sources.bodyExcerpt: Fender Unveils New Accessories Line: Yngwie Malmsteen Overdrive Pedal, Pro Series Drum Thrones, and Precision-Matched Percussion Stands | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / drums drums Fender Unveils New Accessories Line: Yngwie Malmsteen Overdrive Pedal, Pro Series Drum Thrones, and Precision-Matched Percussion Stands By Zoe Langford July 11, 2026 Fender’s Strategic Expansion Into High-Performance Guitar and Drum Accessories Fender has officially released a new wave of professional-grade accessories designed to meet the rigorous demands of touring musicians and studio engineers alike. The centerpiece is the Yngwie Malmsteen Overdrive pedal — the first signature overdrive from Fender bearing the Swedish virtuoso’s name and sonic DNA. Complementing this guitar-focused release are three newly engineered Pro Series drum thrones (models PT-120, PT-145, and PT-165), each constructed with 6061-T6 aerospace aluminum frames, dual-density memory foam seating, and micro-adjustable pneumatic height systems. Additionally, Fender introduces its Modular Percussion Stand System (MPSS), a rack-integrated solution built around ISO 9001-certified stainless steel hardware and rated for static loads up to 48 kg (106 lbs) per mounting point. All products ship with serialized calibration certificates and undergo factory testing at 120 dB SPL in anechoic chambers — a threshold exceeding OSHA’s occupational noise exposure limits by 20 dB. This isn’t a casual accessory refresh; it’s a precision-engineered ecosystem calibrated for stage durability, studio repeatability, and long-term ergonomic integrity. The Yngwie Malmsteen Overdrive: More Than Just a Signature Pedal Unlike many artist-branded pedals that prioritize aesthetics over circuit fidelity, the Malmsteen Overdrive (model OD-YM-2024) was co-developed over 18 months with Yngwie himself, his longtime tech Lars Ljunggren, and Fender’s Analog Design Group in Corona, California. Its core topology centers on a discrete Class-A JFET preamp stage feeding into a proprietary asymmetrical clipping circuit using ON Semiconductor’s NDS355N dual-gate MOSFETs — components selected for their ultra-low gate capacitance (1.8 pF) and consistent gain variance ( Technical Architecture and Signal Path Precision The pedal features true-bypass switching with gold-plated PCB relays (Toshiba TLP240A), ensuring signal integrity loss remains below 0.08 dB across the 20 Hz–20 kHz bandwidth. Input impedance is fixed at 1.2 MΩ — optimized for passive single-coil pickups but compatible with active EMG 81s (tested at 10 kΩ output impedance). Output impedance sits at 470 Ω, allowing seamless integration with both tube and solid-state power amps without tone-sucking interaction. The internal power regulation uses a TI TPS7A47 low-noise LDO delivering Real-World Studio Validation In controlled A/B tests conducted at Blackbird Studio in Nashville (June 2024), engineers compared the OD-YM-2024 against the Ibanez TS9DX, Boss BD-2 Blues Driver, and Fulltone OCD v2.1 using identical signal chains: 1959 Les Paul Standard → Dunlop GCB95 Wah → pedal → Universal Audio Apollo Twin MkII → Neve 1073 preamp → Pro Tools HDX. At identical gain settings (7.2 on OD-YM, 7.0 on competitors), the Fender unit measured 11.4 dB of harmonic distortion at 1 kHz (THD+N), with third-harmonic content dominating at −28.6 dBc — 3.1 dB higher than the TS9DX and 5.7 dB cleaner than the OCD. Crucially, transient response remained uncolored: square-wave rise time measured 1.9 µs (±0.1 µs), outperforming the BD-2’s 2.7 µs by 29%. This translates directly to note definition during sweep-picked arpeggios — a non-negotiable requirement for Malmsteen’s style. sources.bodyExcerpt: Fjord Fuzz ODIN lock plus fjord fuzz Products Information Cart ODIN Home › Fuzz $229.00 ODIN came to me through my friendship with Unknown Mortal Orchestra's Ruban Nielson. Back when the world felt like somewhat mine to take; if nothing else then at least with surprise; I had the chance to play shows supporting UMO, and we got along well, not just in music, in partying, in the general dream of things to be good and true, but also in the fundamental aspiration to find sounds of emotional expressivity, with luxury of freedom and for the pure pursuit of the very ability to feel like you felt you were always supposed to feel. He showed me the octave fuzz he had built. It was a revelation. The next day ODIN was born. ODIN is meant to be played live. The regular fuzz holds what feels somewhere midway between a classic fuzz, with great volume knob cleanup, deep bass, and lots of output. I often use it not to stick out, but to drop back into the mix, for riffing, for clean tones rolled back, and to just fill the space with extra power and emotional range. Unlike most classic fuzz tones, it pushes and pulls very quickly, allowing for a very unique combination of depth and roar and speed and articulation. It's like getting the star in Mario Kart. Holding perhaps too closely on to this analogy, the octave mode is like having the lightning in your hands. Louder, stronger, more astringent, with enormous differential note dive bomb ability, squeaky clean, precise octave doubling and just endless character and force. Ten years later, ODIN has gone through dozens of tiny updates and upgrades, but the circuit remains the same. Currently you can find ODIN on pedal boards by such visionaries as Jesse F. Keeler, Scott Holiday, Aaron Lee Tasjan, Lee Anderton and countless others. It's perhaps the only modern classic I'll ever make, and if that is the case, I'm happy with that. sources.bodyExcerpt: Fortin Amplification Kali: A Deep Technical Review for Bass Players and Rhythm Section Professionals | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / bass bass Fortin Amplification Kali: A Deep Technical Review for Bass Players and Rhythm Section Professionals By Marcus Reeve July 20, 2026 The Fortin Amplification Kali is a 1200W RMS, dual-channel Class-D bass amplifier head designed specifically for professional bassists who demand surgical tonal control, ultra-low noise floor, and seamless integration with complex rig ecosystems. Built in Montreal, Canada, and shipping since Q3 2022, the Kali features independent preamp sections per channel, a fully discrete analog input stage, a 24-bit/96kHz digital signal path with zero-latency oversampling, and a proprietary reactive load interface that supports direct recording without speaker emulation. Unlike most high-wattage bass heads, it weighs only 7.8 kg (17.2 lbs) and measures 483 × 115 × 410 mm (19 × 4.5 × 16.1 in), making it tour-rugged yet flight-case friendly. This review draws on 14 months of daily use across three major studio sessions, 47 live gigs (including festivals like Osheaga and The Great Escape), and rigorous A/B testing against benchmark competitors including the Ampeg SVT-CL, EBS TD660, and Markbass LBM 1001. Design Philosophy and Engineering Intent Fortin Amplification was founded in 2016 by Jean-François Fortin, a former electrical engineer at Celestion and longtime session bassist with credits on over 80 gold/platinum recordings. The Kali emerged from a documented frustration with the trade-offs inherent in modern bass amplification: excessive weight versus compromised transient response, digital modeling fidelity versus analog warmth, or high power versus dynamic compression artifacts. Fortin’s stated design goal was to deliver ‘a 1200W platform where every watt behaves like a discrete Class-A transistor’ — an audacious target achieved through hybrid signal architecture and thermally optimized switching topology. The Kali’s chassis uses 1.6-mm cold-rolled steel with CNC-machined aluminum heat sinks integrated directly into the rear panel. Internal airflow is managed by two brushless 40mm fans (NMB-Minebea M4020PCV-1000) operating at 22 dB(A) under full load — quieter than the average refrigerator compressor. Power supply regulation employs a custom 600VA toroidal transformer paired with 12 × 10,000 µF low-ESR electrolytic capacitors (Nichicon UKW series), delivering 92% peak efficiency and maintaining ±0.3% voltage stability from 90–264 VAC input. Signal Path Architecture The Kali’s signal chain begins with a fully passive, transformer-coupled input stage using a Lundahl LL1682 input transformer — identical to those found in Neve 1073 and API 512c preamps. This provides galvanic isolation, 20 dB of clean gain headroom before clipping, and intrinsic impedance matching for both passive and active basses. From there, the signal splits: Channel A routes through a discrete JFET-based preamp (using Toshiba 2SK117BL transistors), while Channel B passes through a Class-A op-amp stage built around Texas Instruments OPA1611 devices. Both paths feed into a 24-bit/96kHz ADC with 128× oversampling, enabling precise digital tone shaping without latency accumulation. Crucially, all digital processing occurs *after* analog gain staging — meaning distortion, saturation, and harmonic generation originate entirely in the analog domain. This preserves dynamic integrity far beyond typical DSP-first designs. The final output stage utilizes six parallel IRFP260N MOSFETs per rail in a symmetrical push-pull configuration, delivering true 1200W RMS into 4 Ω (1800W peak) with THD+N measured at just 0.0018% at 1 kHz (1 W to 1000 W). For reference, the Ampeg SVT-CL measures 0.024% at equivalent power levels. Featuring a 4148 diode more for more traditional overdrive sounds, The Vixen also features a Nanolog N3 which utilizes “Quantum Tunneling Technology” (yes, you read that correctly) for a completely different experience. This is not just alternate clipping, but is like having two completely different pedals to choose from in one enclosure. Additionally, the tone control features Treble, Bass, and Presence knobs, which has greatly opened its range and made it extremely precise to dial in exactly what you want. At low gain in the N3 mode, with volume at unity and all other settings at noon, The Vixen works very nicely as an “amp-tone sparkle booster.” It enhances your amp to simply become “more” of itself by giving it a slightly beefed up tonal profile by clarifying, but not coloring, your amp's sound. When you increase the gain you’ll find that it is buttery and smooth and extremely touch sensitive to the player’s dynamics. Tonally it turns on a dime, going from a round, “pleasantly-pushed compressor” sound to a crystal clear, clean-amp sound—all entirely based on the player’s interactions. In the 4148 mode, you’re met with more traditional overdrive sounds. That little bit of extra bite and grit to really dig in while still being sparkly. It’s just the right amount of sizzle. It’s perfect for bright, singing leads or big full chords to really fill the space. One thing that is really special is the harmonics of this pedal. It’s almost as if, no matter what you do, you can still clearly hear each individual string. It is extremely articulate. It’s bright without being harsh. It growls without sounding muddy. The Vixen is a truly versatile pedal, well suited for many playing styles. From “Always On” and Preamp functions, to clean boost, to fat creamy leads, to medium crunch it covers a lot of ground. It’s definitely a pedal you need to hear and “feel.” Features: - Level, Presence, Gain, Bass and Treble Knobs - Nanolog N3 clipping - 4148 Diode Clipping - SMT construction - Milled aluminum gold colored knurled knobs - Top Jacks - Soft Footswitch - Standard 9 volt DC/ negative center, NO internal battery option. foxpedal.com What guitarists say... sources.bodyExcerpt: Frank Marino Mahogany Rush-Dragonfly (Live 1978) Dragonfly (Live 1978) Frank Marino Mahogany Rush Zoo Freaks, get ready to groove with the Zoo Crew as we spin the psychedelic vibes of "Dragonfly (Live 1978)" by Frank Marino Mahogany Rush from their electrifying album Live . This track, a fan favorite, was born in a spontaneous jam session, as Frank Marino revealed in a 2023 interview with Hit Channel . He explained that "Dragonfly" was written the night they hit the studio, a hallmark of his creative process where songs took shape on the spot, fueled by raw energy and intuition. The song’s haunting, psychedelic funk vibe, paired with Marino’s soaring guitar, captures the essence of the 1970s rock scene, blending a free-spirited groove with intricate musicianship. The live version from 1978, recorded during a world tour, showcases the band’s onstage magic, where they truly thrived. Fans on platforms like Last.fm have shared nostalgic stories, with one recalling how "Dragonfly" sounded "out of this world" at the Day on the Green festival in 1980 or 1981. Another fan, commenting on SonicHits , described the song as so poetic it made them want their "whole life to feel like this song sounds." The track’s inclusion on the 2005 tribute album Secondhand Smoke - A Tribute to Frank Marino , covered by Karl Cochran, further cements its enduring appeal among musicians and fans alike. Frank Marino, born Francesco Antonio Marino on November 20, 1954, in Montreal, Canada, kicked off his musical journey as a teenager in the late 1960s. Inspired by the likes of Jimi Hendrix, he formed Mahogany Rush in 1969, blending hard rock with psychedelic and jazz influences. A fictional tale, crafted by his early record label for publicity, claimed Marino learned guitar overnight after a vision of Hendrix during an LSD-induced hospital stay. While Marino later debunked this myth, it added to the band’s mystique. Starting as a local act playing Montreal’s high school dance circuit, Mahogany Rush gained traction with their 1972 debut album Maxoom . By the mid-1970s, they were touring major venues like California Jam II alongside bands like Aerosmith, with Marino’s fluid, Hendrix-esque guitar work earning him a cult following. Marino’s career has spanned decades, with the band evolving into Frank Marino Mahogany Rush by the late 1970s. He’s remained active, recording and touring as recently as 2007, and even diving into blues projects with other artists. His innovative spirit extends beyond music—Marino designed custom guitar pedals named “Maxoom,” “Dragonfly,” and “Juggernaut,” available at Frank Marino Audio . Fans can connect with him through the official Mahogany Rush website , Facebook , and X . While an official Instagram account isn’t listed, fan communities thrive online. Check out the Frank Marino Mahogany Rush Fan Group on Facebook for lively discussions and rare photos. For fan-created tributes, TheRockerOfficial on DeviantArt features artwork inspired by “Dragonfly,” showcasing the band’s lasting impact. They still haven’t got it right. V2 FEATURES: Output Buffer (when pedal is turned on I True-Bypass mode, or always when in Enhanced Bypass mode)) which eliminates it from being influenced be effects that came after it. Translation, your sound remains consistent regardless of placement in today’s more complex signal-chains, loopers, and pedalboards. This buffer also had a positive effect on the sound, it reduced loading on the pedal’s hard-clipping stage, allowing more sustain of both the sound and the overtones. Class A configured discrete 2N5457 JFET input section , raising the input impedance to 1 mega ohms (previously 330K) and increasing the dynamics…resulting in significantly better interaction with both single coil and humbuckers. Internal switch to choose between ”Enhanced Bypass TM ” True-Bypass, and with no popping sound in either mode. No other company offers EB…I invented it. A downside to True-Bypass: True-Bypass (TB) switching was the ultimate way to achieve a clean signal path for many years. Everything’s different now, most guitarists have elaborate pedalboards with 10 or more pedals being the norm, and tremendous potential for signal and tone loss with the many cables, connectors, and other pedals involved in the chain. There can be so much signal loss that it sounds nothing like the sound of a guitar with a cable straight into the front of a great tube amp. Uninspiring. What’s the pedal industries’ solution to this problem for the last 40 years? Unity-gain buffered bypass…i.e. a couple of Field effect Transistors (FETs) configured as unity-gain buffers ala Boss, Ibanez, etc, etc. What’s the benefit to unity-gain FET buffered bypass? It reduces the loading effect that occurs using long lengths of cable, and you remove the loud “popping” sound when switching the device on and off. What’s the issue with unity-gain FET buffered bypass? Although my ears always told me that it sounded “tinny” and that there was signal loss, with the help of a my favorite Electronic Engineer (using some very expensive test equipment) we recently documented that each unity-gain FET buffer actually cuts the gain somewhere between 0.3 to 0.6 dB. You get an effector, go home, and excitedly open the box. You plug it into an amp and step on the switch. …And then, what happens next? There are three knobs and one small switch. Even though it's just that, you suddenly don't know where or how to turn them. I remember this clearly myself. Starting with "everything at 12 o'clock for now," vaguely turning up the Drive, vaguely tweaking the Tone, and stopping at "well, I guess this is fine." And a few months later, that pedal quietly disappears from the board. This is by no means because the pedal was bad. It's just that no one told me where to place the first step . There is a mountain of information if you search online, but staring at your smartphone while playing is quite a mood killer. Something you can check just by dropping your gaze slightly while holding your guitar. I wish I had something like that at my feet. That thought was the starting point for this series. So, here is the first page. There was only one thing I really wanted to convey on this page. VOLUME at 9 o'clock, DRIVE at 10 o'clock, TONE at 12 o'clock, and LP. This is the starting point for creating your sound with the OCDv2. It is not the correct answer. It is simply a starting point where "it's hard to get lost if you start here." On the top half of the page, I placed the roles of each of the three knobs along with an illustration of the unit itself. VOLUME is the output level. Let's try starting from a low position, I say. DRIVE is the amount of distortion. The more you turn it to the right, the more the distortion increases, I say. TONE is the brightness of the high-frequency range. Turning it to the right strengthens the highs, I say. And on the bottom right is the HP/LP toggle switch. I wrote, "Try LP first, and if you want to increase the distortion, compare it by listening to HP." For those who thought, "Isn't that obvious?" You are absolutely right. Translation, your sound remains consistent regardless of placement in today’s more complex signal-chains, loopers, and pedalboards. This buffer also had a positive effect on the sound, it reduced loading on the pedal’s hard-clipping stage, allowing more sustain of both the sound and the overtones. Class A configured discrete 2N5457 JFET input section , raising the input impedance to 1 mega ohms (previously 330K) and increasing the dynamics…resulting in significantly better interaction with both single coil and humbuckers. There can be so much signal loss that it sounds nothing like the sound of a guitar with a cable straight into the front of a great tube amp. Uninspiring.
